name: Losoong masked dance at Phodong
summary: Losoong is the Sikkimese harvest new year, celebrated by Bhutias and, as Namsoong, by Lepchas. Before it, Phodong and Rumtek monasteries hold masked chaam dances that tell stories of Guru Padmasambhava and end with the burning of an effigy of evil.
body: Losoong, also called Sonam Losoong, marks the end of the harvest. It falls on the first day of the eleventh month of the Tibetan calendar, usually in December, and it is the time when farmers celebrate the year's crops with family and friends. Lepchas celebrate the same season as Namsoong, their new year. The festival borrows much of its ritual from Losar, the Tibetan New Year.

In the days before Losoong, masked dances, or chaam, are held at Phodong Monastery, as well as at Rumtek. Monks in brocade costumes and painted masks perform the dances, which depict episodes from the life of Guru Padmasambhava, called Guru Ugyen in Sikkim, and the victory of good over evil. The dance ends with an effigy of a demon king being burned.

Phodong is small, so the crowd is mostly local families in their best clothes, with monks, children, food stalls and a lot of tea. Arrive early for a good place in the courtyard. Dates change every year with the lunar calendar; confirm with the monastery or Sikkim Tourism, and check current status before you travel.
tips: Arrive by 8–9 am for a place in the courtyard; the best spots fill early.
Dress warmly; December mornings in Phodong are cold, and you will stand for hours.
Do not walk across the dance area or use flash; ask monks before close-up photos.

faqs.q: When is the Losoong chaam at Phodong?
faqs.a: Usually in December, in the days before Losoong, which falls on the first day of the eleventh Tibetan month. The exact dates change every year. Confirm with Phodong Monastery or Sikkim Tourism a few weeks before, and check current status before you travel.

Losoong is the Sikkimese harvest new year, celebrated by Bhutias in December; Lepchas celebrate it as Namsoong. Families gather, special food and drink are prepared, and monasteries such as Phodong and Rumtek hold masked dances before it. It draws on the traditions of the Tibetan New Year, Losar.

faqs.q: Can tourists watch the Phodong masked dance?
faqs.a: Yes. Visitors are welcome to watch from the courtyard edges. Dress modestly, stay off the dance ground, keep voices low and do not use flash. Photography rules may vary during rituals; follow monks' instructions.

faqs.q: How do I get to Phodong for the chaam?
faqs.a: Take an early shared jeep from Gangtok's Vajra stand toward Phodong or Mangan, about ₹120–200 and 1.5 hours, or hire a taxi for about ₹2,500–3,500 for the day. Jeeps fill fast on festival days, so go to the stand by 7 am.

name: Losar in Lachung and Lachen
image_query: Losar Tibetan New Year Sikkim celebration
summary: Losar, the Tibetan New Year, is the biggest festival of the Bhutia villages of Lachung and Lachen. Families clean and decorate their homes, visit the monastery, share food and drink and gather with relatives. In deep winter, it is the village at its warmest.
body: The Lachungpas and Lachenpas are Bhutias, and Losar, the Tibetan New Year, is their most important festival of the year. It falls on the first day of the first Tibetan lunar month, usually in February or early March. Celebrations last several days, beginning with the cleaning of houses and the preparation of special food, and continuing with prayers, family visits and community gatherings.

Homes are decorated, butter lamps are lit, and families visit Lachung Monastery or Lachen's Ngodrub Choling gompa to offer prayers and receive blessings. Prayer flags are renewed on rooftops and ridges. Relatives who live in Gangtok or beyond often come home if the road allows. Food is generous: noodle soups, meat dishes, fried breads and home-made drinks.

Visitors are rare in these weeks, because it is deep winter and the road is often closed by snow. If you are in Lachung or Lachen at Losar, you are a guest at a family festival, not a show. Ask your host what is appropriate, accept food when offered, and check current status before you travel.
tips: Ask your homestay host before visiting the monastery during Losar rituals.
Bring a small gift such as fruit or sweets if you are invited into a home.
Plan spare days; snow can close the Lachung and Lachen roads around Losar.

faqs.a: Losar falls on the first day of the first month of the Tibetan lunar calendar, usually in February or early March. Celebrations in Lachung and Lachen last several days. Dates change every year; check the Tibetan calendar and confirm with your homestay or agent.

faqs.q: Can tourists join Losar celebrations in Lachung?
faqs.a: Tourists staying in Lachung or Lachen at Losar may be invited to share food and see family and monastery celebrations, but it is a private, religious festival, not a staged event. Ask your host what is appropriate and follow their lead.

Usually, but Losar falls in winter, when snow can close the road to Lachung, and especially beyond to Yumthang and Zero Point. Tours may run with few passengers. Keep flexible dates and check current status before you travel.

faqs.q: What food is eaten at Losar?
faqs.a: Families prepare generous meals: noodle soups, meat dishes, momos, fried breads and sweets, along with butter tea and home-made drinks. Each family has its own specialities. If you stay in a homestay, you may get a taste of the festival meal.

name: Kamsel at Tholung Monastery
when: April, once every three years (Tibetan calendar)
summary: Every three years, the sacred relics hidden at Tholung Monastery in upper Dzongu during the Gorkha invasions are taken out of their sealed boxes, aired and shown to the public. Pilgrims walk in from across Sikkim for the Kamsel ceremony.
body: Tholung Monastery, built in 1789 in remote upper Dzongu, became a refuge in the late 18th century when Gorkha armies from Nepal invaded Sikkim. Manuscripts, images and relics from other monasteries were carried to Tholung for safekeeping, along with a metal chorten holding the ashes of an incarnation of Lhatsun Chenpo. They have been kept in more than a dozen sealed boxes ever since.

Because of the damp forest climate, the relics are taken out once every three years to be aired and sunned. This is the Kamsel ceremony, held in April and supervised by the Sikkim government's Ecclesiastical Department, whose role began in the 1940s. During Kamsel the relics are displayed to worshippers, who come from all over Sikkim, many walking the last stretch through the forest.

It is a pilgrimage rather than a festival with dances. Facilities are basic and crowded. Plan through a Dzongu homestay, which can advise on permits, transport and the walk in. The Kamsel year and dates must be confirmed in advance; check current status before you travel.
tips: Confirm the Kamsel year and dates with a Dzongu homestay or Sikkim Tourism well in advance.
Get your Dzongu permit early; demand rises in a Kamsel year.
Walk slowly, carry water and a rain jacket, and wear leech socks on the forest path.

faqs.a: Kamsel is the airing and public display of the sacred relics kept at Tholung Monastery in upper Dzongu. Held every three years in April, it lets the damp-sensitive relics be ventilated and allows pilgrims to see and be blessed by them. The Ecclesiastical Department of Sikkim oversees it.

faqs.q: How often is the Tholung Kamsel held?
faqs.a: Once every three years, in April. The precise dates follow the Tibetan calendar and are announced in advance. Ask a Dzongu homestay or Sikkim Tourism which year the next Kamsel falls in and check current status before you travel.

faqs.q: Can tourists attend the Tholung Kamsel?
faqs.a: Respectful visitors with a valid Dzongu permit can usually attend, but it is a religious occasion, crowded and basic. Plan transport and the walk in through a homestay, dress modestly and follow the monks' instructions on photography.

faqs.q: How do I reach Tholung Monastery for Kamsel?
faqs.a: From Mangan, cross into Dzongu with your permit and travel by car up the upper Dzongu road, then walk the last stretch through forest. Roads and paths change after landslides, so a local guide from your homestay is the best plan.
